new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Stress in Kumyk is dynamic; as a rule it falls on the last syllable of the stem, and when an affix is added to the stem it moves onto the affix. [...] 2.2.2. The nominal affix -ma is opposed in its accentual properties to the negative verbal affix of the imperative mood: jazmá 'manuscript' vs. jázma 'don't write'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (expiratory) word stress on the final syllable of the word: stem-final in bare stems, shifting rightward onto each added suffix, i.e. regular word-final stress; certain affixes (the verbal negative -ma of the imperative) do not take the stress, leaving it on the preceding stem syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged 'как правило' (as a rule); explicit exception: negative imperative -ma is unstressed (я́зма 'don't write') vs. stressed nominal -ма (язма́ 'manuscript'). No list of other unstressable affixes/clitics or loanword exceptions is given in this sketch.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word (stem + affixes); examples are citation forms; no discussion of phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Levitskaja 1997 describes standard/literary Kumyk (based on the Bujnaksk and Xasavjurt dialects, per her sec. 1.3.2), i.e. kumy1244 at language level; she notes (1.6.0) that Kajtak and Podgornyj dialects show contact features (ejectives, harmony violations) but says nothing dialect-specific about stress.
